content: More than one million curable sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are acquired globally every day. These infections are primarily caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Treponema pallidum (syphilis), and Trichomonas vaginalis. Additionally, over one in seven women worldwide are estimated to be infected with human papillomavirus (HPV), which is a leading cause of cervical cancer. Furthermore, more than 500 million people are living with genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) infections. Certain population groups are particularly vulnerable to STIs. These include sex workers and their clients, men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender and gender-diverse individuals, adolescents and young adults, mobile populations, and individuals affected by conflict and civil unrest. The Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) on HIV, Hepatitis, and STIs aims to eliminate STIs as public health concerns by 2030. This includes reducing the number of new curable STI cases by 90% compared to 2020 levels and reducing congenital syphilis cases to fewer than 50 per 100,000 live births annually, representing an 88% decline from 2020. Achieving these targets will require significant scaling up of resources for STI prevention and treatment, as well as investment in new diagnostic, prevention, and treatment technologies. Strengthening national health systems to collect and analyze STI data in a timely manner is also essential. This data will inform health policies, treatment guidelines, and resource allocation. Key data to be collected includes case reports of symptomatic infections, testing data, prevalence surveys, etiological assessments of STI syndromes, and monitoring of gonococcal antimicrobial resistance. Diagnosing and treating STIs is a critical component of HIV prevention and treatment services. Surveillance of STIs, such as urethral discharge and gonorrhea in men or primary and secondary syphilis, can serve as an early warning of the potential for HIV epidemics in specific populations. It also provides insight into ongoing high-risk sexual behaviors that may require intensified intervention programs. There is a high co-prevalence of HIV and other STIs, particularly in vulnerable populations. Many of these infections, especially among women, are asymptomatic. STIs significantly increase the transmissibility of HIV and the risk of acquiring HIV by up to 2–3 times in some populations. This increased risk is due to STI-related sores or inflammation, which compromise the protective barrier of intact skin, and increased HIV shedding in individuals with HIV who have urethritis, genital ulcers, or Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections. Genital herpes (HSV-2) nearly triples the risk of acquiring HIV for both men and women. Additionally, HIV exacerbates the infectiousness and severity of STIs, and co-infection with HIV and syphilis can negatively impact immune recovery and antiretroviral therapy effectiveness. Prompt diagnosis and treatment of STIs can help reduce HIV transmission. Individuals seeking STI testing or treatment represent a population at increased risk for HIV, providing an opportunity for HIV screening. Moreover, providing STI services to people living with HIV is part of a comprehensive approach to sexual and reproductive health and rights. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations for STI screening and treatment. For men who have sex with men and transgender individuals, periodic testing for asymptomatic urethral and rectal Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis infections using molecular assays is suggested. Periodic serological testing for asymptomatic syphilis is strongly recommended. For sex workers in lowand middle-income countries, periodic screening for asymptomatic STIs is suggested. For pregnant women, WHO recommends screening all for syphilis during their first antenatal care visit. For symptomatic STIs, WHO recommends management based on molecular assay results where available. In settings with limited or no molecular testing capacity, syndromic treatment is recommended to ensure same-day treatment. For individuals with urethral discharge, vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain, genital ulcers, or anorectal discharge, treatment should be guided by either molecular assays, rapid point-of-care tests, or syndromic diagnosis, depending on the available resources. STI data collection and reporting are critical for monitoring appropriate treatment and informing public health strategies. This includes data from HIV prevention services, community outreach programs, HIV testing and treatment clinics, and key population programs. Priority indicators for STIs, such as syphilis and gonorrhea, should be integrated into HIV surveillance systems. In countries where data on other STIs, such as chlamydia and trichomoniasis, are collected, similar indicators should be considered. Viral hepatitis, particularly hepatitis B (HBV) and hepatitis C (HCV), also represents a significant global health burden, causing over one million deaths annually due to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. In 2019, an estimated 296 million people were living with chronic HBV infection, and 58 million with HCV infection. The burden of viral hepatitis is concentrated in specific geographic regions and populations, including economically disadvantaged areas, displaced populations, migrants, rural communities, and people who inject drugs. Health care workers exposed to needle-stick injuries, incarcerated individuals, and men who have sex with men are also at increased risk. HIV, HBV, and HCV infections can be prevented through interventions such as reducing mother-to-child transmission, ensuring blood safety, adhering to universal precautions in healthcare settings, promoting safer sex practices, and implementing harm reduction strategies for people who inject drugs. Co-infection with HIV and viral hepatitis accelerates the progression to liver disease, hepatocellular carcinoma, and death. Pregnant women living with HIV have twice the risk of vertical transmission of HBV. Vulnerable populations co-infected with HIV and viral hepatitis face additional challenges, including limited access to healthcare services and stigma. A comprehensive, person-centered approach is essential in settings where individuals are at substantial risk of both viral hepatitis and HIV. This ensures that high-risk individuals receiving HIV prevention services also receive hepatitis screening and care.
